headline: AI agents produced checkable proofs of two famous math problems, and scientists got a dedicated AI workbench that records how every result was made.
summary_for_scientists: Two labs showed coordinated AI agents doing multi-day scientific reasoning that a computer can verify line by line, including a result about the equations that govern fluid flow. Anthropic released Claude Science, a research environment that keeps the code, environment, and history behind every figure. The practical shift: AI work that can be checked and reproduced, which is the standard researchers already hold themselves to.

lab_pick.title: Claude Science, an AI workbench for scientists
lab_pick.what_they_did: Anthropic built a research app around a coordinating agent with more than 60 curated skills and connectors, including cheminformatics and structural biology. It runs locally on macOS or Linux, over SSH, or from an HPC login node.
lab_pick.result: Every figure comes with the exact code, the environment, a plain-language description, and the full message history that produced it. A reviewer agent checks citations and calculations and flags errors.
lab_pick.why_researchers_care: It answers the first question a skeptical scientist asks about AI output: how was this made, and can I reproduce it? Molecules and chemical structures render natively, so it's closer to the bench than a chat window.
lab_pick.how_to_share: Demo it in a lab meeting on a dataset the team already knows, and open the history behind one figure. Anthropic is also backing up to 50 AI-for-science projects with up to $30,000 in credits each, running September 1 to December 1, 2026.

sections.title: Lab Automation & Scientific Reasoning
sections.description: Agents doing long, verifiable scientific work.

items.title: On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem
items.one_line: OpenAI says an internal system of roughly 10,000 agents produced, in 88 hours, a proof that the Navier–Stokes equations for fluid motion can develop a singularity in finite time. It shared a written proof and a Lean formalization.
items.try_this: Anyone who models airflow or heat transfer works with these equations. Ask the team what they'd hand to an agent crew if a week of compute were free.

items.title: Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem
items.one_line: Claude worked largely autonomously for 11 days, with dozens of agents collaborating, to produce the first complete computer-checked proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean.
items.try_this: Use it as the example of AI output that's verified by a machine rather than trusted on faith.

items.title: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous Interpretability Research?
items.one_line: A new benchmark tests whether AI agents can run an end-to-end research loop on their own, from hypothesis to experiment to analysis, in one area of AI research.
items.try_this: Borrow the structure: write down the research loop your team runs most often and mark which steps an agent could take first.

sections.title: Tools Researchers Can Use Now
sections.description: Access and tooling aimed at working scientists.

items.title: Life Sciences Verification Program
items.one_line: Verified life-science teams get Anthropic's top models with safeguards tuned for biology work, usable in Claude Science, Claude.ai, Claude Code, and the API. It's in beta for teams and institutions, with dozens of organizations already onboarded.
items.try_this: A signal that model providers are building verified tracks for specific sciences. Worth watching for chemistry and materials.

try_in_the_lab: Run one familiar dataset through an AI research workbench and compare the generated figure and code with how the team made it by hand.
Pick one simulation or data-reduction step the team repeats every week and time how long an agent takes to reproduce it.
Hold a 20-minute journal club on the Fermat and Navier–Stokes results. Ask what 'machine-checked' would mean for your own results.
coverage_note: A light week for materials and building-science AI. This week was gathered before the science desk launched, so most of the science signal came from mathematical reasoning and research tooling.
